extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, and the public
extracted.subtask_description: An index/table of worked examples illustrating the USPTO's subject-matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101) analysis (Step 1, Step 2A, Step 2B) used by examiners and the public to locate precedent and guidance for eligibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory Category
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the statutory category(ies) recited by the claim (e.g., Process, Machine, Manufacture, Composition, System). The table's Step 1 column lists the statutory category for each example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether the claim falls within a §101 statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition/system). Examples in the table show mappings such as 'Process, CRM (Manufacture)', 'System (Machine or Manufacture)', 'Composition', etc.; examiners use this as the first step of the eligibility flowchart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Judicial Exception (Exception Presence/Type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., Abstract Idea, Product of Nature, Law of Nature) or no exception. The table's Step 2A: Exception column indicates this for each example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion identifies whether the claimed subject matter is a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon/product of nature). Table entries include values like 'Abstract Idea', 'Product of Nature', 'Law of Nature', 'None', and 'n/a' for examples where not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: MDC Analysis (Characteristics of the Exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the characteristic(s) of the judicial exception at issue (e.g., function/activity; chem/phys property; structure or form; transformation; phenotype). The table's Step 2A: MDC Analysis column lists these characteristics for each example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to articulate why a claim is considered to recite the exception by specifying how the exception manifests (for example, 'function/activity, structure or form', 'chem/phys property', 'phenotype', 'transformation'). This helps map a claim's elements to the kind of judicial exception analyzed in Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'Significantly More' Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself. The table's Step 2B column identifies which considerations apply for each example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the §101 second-part inquiry: consider whether the claim adds an inventive concept/meaningfully more beyond the exception. The table annotates which considerations (see separate listed considerations) apply to each example to show why it either passes or fails Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that a claim element or limitation 'improving computer' can weigh in favor of eligibility under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index flags examples where the claim was considered to 'improv[e] computer' as a potentially meaningful limitation supporting eligibility; typically contrasted with generic computer implementation which is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving another technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that a claim element 'improving another technology' can support a finding of significantly more under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's additional elements improve a technology other than computers (i.e., provide a technological solution), this is treated as a meaningful limitation favoring eligibility in the table's annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that non-generic, meaningful limitations (beyond routine, conventional implementation) can supply 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table marks examples where 'other meaningful limitations' (i.e., claim elements that are more than conventional or generic additions) contributed to a positive Step 2B outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (WURC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative/signifying consideration: claim limitations that are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' (often illustrated as 'generic computer performing generic computer functions') weigh against finding 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index repeatedly flags 'limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (generic computer performing generic computer functions)' to indicate why many computer-implemented claims fail Step 2B. Presence of WURC limitations typically supports a non-eligible result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation that is not well-understood, routine, and conventional (non-WURC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive/signifying consideration: claim limitations that are not well-understood, routine, and conventional can support finding 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table marks examples where limitations were specifically identified as not WURC; such limitations may be considered improvements or meaningful additions and thus support eligibility under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to 'apply it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that mere instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea or law of nature (i.e., directing use without adding meaningful limitation) do not supply 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index highlights examples where claims merely instruct to implement/apply the exception (e.g., 'apply it'), indicating such claims fail Step 2B because they add no meaningful limitation beyond the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extrasolution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that trivial or 'insignificant extrasolution activity' added to an exception does not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples flagged with 'insignificant extrasolution activity' illustrate that adding conventional or token physical steps/activities that do not transform the exception are insufficient for Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of limitations that merely recite a field of use (i.e., limiting the abstract idea to a specific field) and whether such a field-of-use limitation contributes 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index marks examples where field-of-use limitations were present and typically treats mere field-of-use restrictions as insufficient (insignificant) unless accompanied by other meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that a physical transformation or change can be a meaningful limitation (e.g., transformation of an article/state) supporting eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MDC Analysis/Step 2B columns annotate examples where transformation (physical change) was relevant; physical transformations can weigh in favor of eligibility when they are central to the claim's added elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine / System
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that reciting a particular machine or an improvement to a machine/system can supply 'significantly more' (and in some examples leads to 'Streamlined (Particular Machine)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table distinguishes examples where recitation of a particular machine or an improvement to it was treated as a meaningful limitation (contrasted with generic computer implementation). Some examples are labeled 'Streamlined (Particular Machine)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined determinations (labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels used in the index such as 'Streamlined (Product of Nature)', 'Streamlined (Particular Machine)', and 'Streamlined (No Exception)' indicate examples where a streamlined eligibility conclusion was reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These shorthand labels indicate examples where the USPTO applied a streamlined determination (i.e., did not require full two-step analysis) because the example clearly fell into a particular outcome (e.g., clearly a product of nature, clearly not an exception, or clearly a particular machine). The index uses these to quickly signal the analysis outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples as quick reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The columns titled Step 1, Step 2A, and Step 2B are intended to provide a brief guide to the concepts illustrated by each example so examiners and the public may quickly locate pertinent examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note on the page states these columns indicate for each example the relevant statutory categories, judicial exceptions, characteristics discussed in the MDC analysis, and considerations evaluated in the significantly more inquiry; they are a navigational/interpretive rubric for selecting examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example indexing and source-document mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: All examples are consecutively numbered in the table and the 'Source Document' column indicates both the source guidance document and the original example number from that document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rubric ensures traceability: examples drawn from multiple source documents (e.g., 'Examples: Abstract Ideas', 'Examples: Nature-Based Products', 'Computer Based Training', 'July 2015 Update', 'Life Sciences') are re-numbered consecutively for easy reference while preserving original source identifiers.
